name: Dwight D. Eisenhower
role: US president (1953-1961); Supreme Allied Commander in Europe; five-star general
summary: Eisenhower described himself as a 'moderate' who sought a middle way: he cut taxes and federal spending and aimed to balance the budget, yet kept and extended social security and the New Deal's core programs and built the interstate highway system. In foreign policy he led the Cold War alliance system and relied on nuclear deterrence and covert action, while pursuing arms control and warning in his farewell of the military-industrial complex. He enforced school desegregation at Little Rock and signed the first civil rights acts since Reconstruction.

universal-healthcare.rationale: In 1954 he said the federal government could help with medical costs while avoiding the 'socialization of medicine'; he proposed federal reinsurance to encourage voluntary private insurance rather than state-guaranteed care.

raise-minimum-wage.rationale: In 1955 he recommended raising the federal minimum wage to ninety cents and extending coverage, repeating the coverage request in 1956; a modest rise rather than a 'substantial' one.

markets-allocate-better.rationale: Asked Congress to reduce federal operations 'in an area where private enterprise can do the job' and praised free enterprise as the dynamic core of the economy.

avoid-deficit-stimulus.rationale: Set a balanced budget as a goal from 1953 and in 1961 warned that deficit financing in prosperous times could erode confidence in the dollar and feed inflation. He did sign a recession housing stimulus in 1958.

cut-welfare.rationale: His record extended social security to ten million more people and unemployment insurance to four million more (1956), and he signed the 1956 Social Security Act; he said parties abolishing social security would not be heard of again. He did not argue welfare creates dependency.

free-trade.rationale: Asked Congress to extend the Reciprocal Trade Agreements Act (renewed 1958) and to join the Organization for Trade Cooperation, to expand trade and remove discrimination against US exports, while keeping safeguards for domestic industries.

tariffs-protect-industry.rationale: Evidence points both ways: he backed reciprocal trade liberalization but said trade policy 'must not ignore legitimate safeguarding of domestic industries, agriculture, and labor standards'.

farm-price-support.rationale: Called for a stable, prosperous agriculture and a farm program in 1954, but in 1960 criticised the basic farm laws as economically distorting; mixed.

restrict-strikes-picketing.rationale: Asked Congress to amend Taft-Hartley (injunction process, secondary boycotts), invoked a Taft-Hartley injunction against the 1959 steel strike, urged protection of third parties from 'blackmail picketing', and signed the Landrum-Griffin Act guaranteeing fair union elections.

decide-locally.rationale: His 1954 letter said the country was 'following a dangerous trend when it permits too great a degree of centralization of governmental functions' and that he opposed it, while accepting federal duties the people expect; he stressed state and local roles.

state-harmful.rationale: Held that the federal government 'cannot avoid or escape responsibilities which the mass of the people firmly believe should be undertaken by it' and expanded social programs.

night-watchman-state.rationale: Created the Department of Health, Education, and Welfare, expanded social security, and launched the interstate highway system, going well beyond defense, justice and property protection.

ban-extremist-parties.rationale: Signed the Communist Control Act of 1954, which outlawed the Communist Party of the United States and barred members from some representative roles.

equal-moral-worth.rationale: He called equal rights for citizens of every race, color and creed a cardinal ideal and desegregated federal activities, but his Executive Order 10450 barred gay people from federal employment.

racial-segregation-law.rationale: Ordered Army schools integrated (1953), reported segregation in the armed forces and federal activities 'on the way out' (1954), and sent federal troops to enforce desegregation at Little Rock (1957), stating segregated public schooling is unconstitutional.

racial-franchise.rationale: Called protecting the right to vote the nation's 'first duty' (1960) and signed the Civil Rights Acts of 1957 empowering federal prosecution of those who deny voting rights.

empower-international-orgs.rationale: Expressed strong support for the UN, proposed an atomic agency under UN auspices, and wanted 'rule of law' to replace 'rule of force', including re-examining the US reservation on the International Court of Justice; he did not call for giving the UN more power as such.

collective-defense.rationale: Built the alliance system: security pacts with more than 40 nations including NATO and SEATO (signed 1954), and said no single country can alone defend all nations threatened by communism ('mutual security').

defeat-communism.rationale: Called communism a hostile, atheistic, indefinitely lasting threat and backed containment, covert action and massive retaliation, but also sought a 'chance for peace', the Geneva summit and Camp David talks with Soviet leaders.

military-superiority.rationale: Said US arms must be 'mighty, ready for instant action' so no aggressor would risk attack and stressed retaliatory power; he framed this as deterrence and balance rather than superiority.

empower-police-military.rationale: Kept record peacetime defense spending and said arms must be mighty, but warned in the farewell against unwarranted influence of the military-industrial complex and criticised arms burdens in 'Chance for Peace'.

arms-reduction.rationale: In 1953 said every gun made is 'a theft from those who hunger', proposed disarmament with strict UN control and inspection, and later put forward 'open skies' (1955).

abolish-armed-forces.rationale: Said US arms 'must be mighty, ready for instant action' and kept a permanent large military; proposed reductions only under inspection.

force-without-un.rationale: Sent Marines to Lebanon (1958) at its government's request and asked Congress for authority to use force to defend Formosa (1955) and in the Middle East (1957), without Security Council approval.

arm-foreign-insurgents.rationale: His administration's CIA supported the 1953 Iranian and 1954 Guatemalan coups; Wikipedia says he supported these regime-changing coups. Details of arming insurgents are not in the sources opened.

end-foreign-alliances.rationale: Created and expanded permanent alliances (NATO support, SEATO, bilateral treaties with Japan and Taiwan) and said bases would be kept, e.g. Okinawa 'indefinitely'.

no-foreign-bases.rationale: Concluded a Japan defense agreement with US bases and announced bases in Okinawa would be maintained 'indefinitely'; US bases overseas formed part of his strategy.

stay-neutral-between-blocs.rationale: Led the Western bloc: 'free world's leadership', NATO and SEATO, and said the strength of free peoples lay in unity.

non-intervention.rationale: His administration intervened in Iran, Guatemala (CIA-backed coups) and Lebanon, and the Eisenhower Doctrine offered force to defend states from communist aggression.

territorial-expansion.rationale: In his first inaugural said Americans 'know and observe the difference between world leadership and imperialism'.

national-self-determination.rationale: Said every other nation has the right of 'choosing their own way of life' (1953) and praised Hungarian desire for freedom.

rich-countries-aid-poor.rationale: Proposed in 1953 devoting a substantial percentage of disarmament savings to a world aid and reconstruction fund and sustained the Mutual Security Program, though framed partly as anti-communist strategy.

keep-nuclear-weapons.rationale: Stated the US would maintain a massive capability to strike back with nuclear weapons while seeking disarmament only under effective inspection.

expand-nuclear.rationale: Proposed Atoms for Peace in 1953, signed the Atomic Energy Act of 1954 and pledged uranium for peaceful use, promoting worldwide use of atomic energy.

future-generations.rationale: Warned against 'plundering ... the precious resources of tomorrow' and mortgaging the material assets of grandchildren.

state-promotes-atheism.rationale: Inferred: he condemned a hostile ideology 'atheistic in character' and a rule that 'glorifies atheistic materialism', so he would not favor state promotion of atheism.

unions-good.rationale: His 1952 AFL speech defended unions’ secure, necessary place in industry.

more-religion-public.rationale: His Back-to-God broadcast called for a national campaign renewing religious commitment.

correct-racial-injustice.rationale: 1953 State of the Union pledged to end segregation wherever federal authority extended.

gradual-change.rationale: His Edgar letter urged moderation; Little Rock address defended gradual lawful reform.

experts-over-public.rationale: His farewell address warned that public policy could become captive of a scientific-technological elite and called for an alert and knowledgeable citizenry, while still respecting research.

central-planning.rationale: His Chynoweth correspondence rejected comprehensive state control as an extreme.

democracy-best.rationale: He defended democratic freedoms while personally authorising overthrow of elected Arbenz.

separate-church-state.rationale: He opposed devotional prayer in public schools as violating the First Amendment (1964), but as president called recognition of God the most basic expression of Americanism and led a national back-to-God campaign.

limit-population.rationale: His later statement urged corrective action controlling population growth, superseding earlier governmental reluctance.

dictatorship-of-proletariat.rationale: His 1955 Advertising Council remarks explicitly rejected proletarian dictatorship’s instrumental treatment of people.

harm-principle.rationale: 1954 Transylvania address limited personal rights by the equal rights of others.

reason-over-faith.rationale: His Back-to-God address made religious faith an essential guide to national action.

no-religion-state-schools.rationale: In 1964 he said religion should be taught in schools only as history of its influence on civilization, not as creed, and that school prayer violates the First Amendment.

consent-of-governed.rationale: He credited citizens with granting office but imposed regime change against another elected government.

separated-powers.rationale: His Edgar letter accepted Supreme Court authority defining limits on federal government.

censor-art-for-virtue.rationale: His 1953 Dartmouth remarks opposed book burning but expressly allowed a decency exception.

sovereign-above-law.rationale: Little Rock address explicitly subordinated presidents and executive action to law.

ban-cartels.rationale: 1956 State of the Union demanded checking monopoly and preserving competition.

courts-bound-by-majority.rationale: He enforced federal court orders at Little Rock against local resistance, saying personal opinions about a decision have no bearing on its enforcement.

entrenched-bill-of-rights.rationale: His 1964 school-prayer remarks defended the First Amendment’s binding restriction on public authorities.

elective-rulers.rationale: His Back-to-God address said citizens conferred government office upon ordinary men.

corporate-influence.rationale: No recorded position found: the evidence found addresses a nearby question, not this statement.

holocaust-denial.rationale: His eyewitness Ohrdruf account insisted on preserving proof against later denial of Nazi atrocities.

islam-incompatible.rationale: He expressly welcomed Muslim worship as part of American constitutional tradition and mutual cultural progress.

social-market-economy.rationale: His Middle Way joined market freedom with public security against poverty.

rent-control.rationale: He ended the Korean War federal controls on prices, wages and rents as one of his first acts and defended the decision to his brother.

politics-spiritual-struggle.rationale: He described the Cold War as a great ideological struggle between spiritual values and a materialistic, godless tyranny.

person-over-state.rationale: His Back-to-God address said government exists to secure pre-existing personal rights.

spiritual-nature.rationale: 1954 Transylvania address placed spiritual human values above mere material advancement.

defensive-wars-only.rationale: He publicly limited force to defence of America’s way of life but personally authorised a foreign paramilitary coup.

collective-bargaining.rationale: His 1954 labor message endorsed the Wagner Act's protection of the right to bargain collectively and a legal framework for free collective bargaining.

no-business-privileges.rationale: No recorded position found: the evidence found addresses a nearby question, not this statement.

notes:
Not reached: his memoirs (Mandate for Change, Waging Peace, Crusade in Europe), the Interstate Highway statements beyond the timeline, the 1954 domino press conference, Brown v. Board and McCarthy remarks, Operation Wetback and the 1954 Pledge of Allegiance statements; these topics stay null. Signed-law and covert-action answers rest on the UCSB timeline and Wikipedia.

Merged with an independent gpt-6.1-sol audit: 32 answers taken from it, 24 agreed, 1 conflicts settled by the integrator.

gpt-6.1-sol notes: Independent full-list pass; no inference. Five priorities answered: public religion, church–state separation, nondevotional state schools, spiritual humanity and faith’s role in action. God-given rights are not treated as divine rather than popular political authority. Later school-prayer views and later population-policy change are used. Equality and democracy claims are qualified by his own security exclusions and personally approved covert intervention. No individual CIA assassination proposal is assumed personally approved by him. Civilian-employment restrictions are not a criminal homosexuality law or military-service rule. Illegal-migration enforcement is not treated as opposition to immigration levels. Full 1954 and 1959 public-paper volumes and all State of the Union addresses downloaded and searched by theme. Cultural and religious history instruction is distinguished from teaching religious creed. All 490 statements and remaining nulls reviewed. Main lane decides inclusion and legacy-list changes.
